title: Status epilepticus in children (India)
specialty: Paediatrics / Paediatric Neurology / Emergency Medicine / Critical Care

evidenceAudit.scope: Convulsive status epilepticus (SE) in infants and children (beyond the newborn period) in India: definitions, prehospital rescue medicines, time-based hospital algorithm, intensive care unit (ICU) treatment of refractory SE, supportive care and investigations, built on the IAP Standard Treatment Guidelines (2022) with the ICMR AES in Children STW. Neonatal seizures and adult SE have separate topics.
findings: ILAE timings (t1 5 minutes, t2 30 minutes for convulsive SE), causes, prehospital buccal or intranasal midazolam 0.1–0.2 mg/kg, lorazepam and rectal diazepam doses, first-line IV doses with maximums, second-line phenytoin, fosphenytoin, valproate, phenobarbitone and levetiracetam doses and rates, refractory midazolam, phenobarbitone, propofol and thiopentone regimens, investigations and monitoring checked against IAP STG 2022.
Matching first- and second-line doses (lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg, midazolam 0.2 mg/kg, phenytoin 20 mg/kg at 1 mg/kg/min) checked against the ICMR AES in Children STW (2019).
unverifiedSections: IAP does not rank second-line drugs; phenytoin is listed first by ICMR and is marked preferred.

Maintenance doses after loading are taken from the US labels (Drugs.com), dextrose from the BC status epilepticus guideline (2011) and pyridoxine from the LHSC NICU manual, because the IAP chapter gives none. Calcium and magnesium replacement follows the electrolyte topics.

IAP gives no limit on the number of benzodiazepine doses; giving no more than two is usual practice. The age criterion for a pyridoxine trial (infants under 2 years) is usual practice; the dose is from LHSC.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Status epilepticus is the commonest neurological emergency in children. A convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer is treated as SE, because seizures beyond 30 minutes are likely to cause lasting neuronal injury (ILAE, quoted by IAP). In Indian children, common causes are febrile seizures, neuroinfection (meningitis, encephalitis, neurocysticercosis), poor adherence in known epilepsy, metabolic derangements and trauma. Treatment is time-based: rescue benzodiazepine at home or at first contact, IV benzodiazepine at 5–20 minutes, a second-line drug at 20–40 minutes, and ICU-based anaesthetic infusions for refractory SE, while correcting hypoglycaemia and finding the cause. Every minute of delay matters: benzodiazepines given within 5–10 minutes stop most seizures, while those given after 30 minutes often fail, which is why rescue medicine at home and fixed time targets in hospital save brain.
keyMechanisms: Failure of seizure-termination mechanisms and excess excitation sustain seizures.
GABA-A receptors are internalised over time, so benzodiazepines work less well the longer SE lasts.
Prolonged seizures cause hypoxia, acidosis, hyperthermia and excitotoxic neuronal injury.
Underlying causes (infection, metabolic, structural) drive recurrence.

symptoms: Eye deviation, nystagmus or subtle twitching after visible jerks stop (non-convulsive SE)
Fever, vomiting or headache before the seizure (neuroinfection)
physicalSigns: Signs of trauma or raised intracranial pressure
redFlags: Seizure continuing after two benzodiazepine doses: second-line drug now
Unstable at the second-line stage or refractory SE: PICU (IAP 2022)
precipitants: Missed antiseizure medicines in known epilepsy (IAP 2022)
Electrolyte or glucose derangement, trauma, toxins (IAP 2022)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Eyes closed and resisting opening, side-to-side head movement, preserved awareness; video EEG settles it.
Shivering with high fever and preserved awareness, no post-ictal state; observation and normal consciousness settle it.
Sustained twisting postures after metoclopramide or antipsychotics with intact awareness; drug history and response to an anticholinergic settle it.
Pallor and a trigger, a few jerks lasting seconds and rapid recovery; history and ECG settle it.
Sweating, drowsiness and seizure in a fasting, ill or diabetic child; bedside glucose settles it.
Decerebrate or decorticate posturing with bradycardia and hypertension, not seizures; CT and pupil examination settle it.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Seizure lasting 5 minutes or more (t1); long-term consequences likely after 30 minutes (t2).
Seizures persisting after benzodiazepine and a second-line drug.
Persisting 24 hours or more after anaesthetic treatment starts.

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Check at once; give glucose if low (IAP 2022).

clinicalManagement.title: First line
actions: IV benzodiazepine; repeat once if seizures continue (IAP 2022).

clinicalManagement.title: Second line
actions: Load one second-line drug (see medicines) (IAP 2022; ICMR AES STW).
Avoid valproate if liver disease or inborn error suspected; avoid phenobarbitone without ventilation backup (IAP 2022).
Already on that drug: at up to phenytoin 6, phenobarbitone 5, valproate 30 or levetiracetam 30 mg/kg/day, give a half dose; at larger doses avoid loading and give the maintenance dose (IAP 2022).

clinicalManagement.title: Refractory SE
actions: PICU with EEG: midazolam infusion, or high-dose phenobarbitone boluses 5–10 mg/kg every 30 minutes (up to 120 mg/kg/24 hours), propofol or thiopentone; enteral topiramate while tapering (IAP 2022).
Treat raised ICP with mannitol or 3% saline; monitor rhabdomyolysis, arrhythmia and sepsis (IAP 2022).

clinicalManagement.title: Find the cause
actions: Teach caregivers first aid and rescue medicine (IAP 2022).

vignette.text: Ishaan, a 2-year-old boy weighing 12 kg, is brought to the emergency department after convulsing for 15 minutes at home. His mother gave no rescue medicine. He has had fever for 2 days. He is still having generalised tonic-clonic movements, SpO2 is 90% on air, and bedside glucose is 4.6 mmol/L. IV access is obtained on the second attempt.

guidedApproach.title: Why benzodiazepines work less with time
guidedApproach.prompt: What changes in the brain as a seizure continues?
guidedApproach.guidance: A seizure normally stops because inhibitory GABA-A mechanisms and other termination processes overcome excitation. In status epilepticus these fail: within minutes, synaptic GABA-A receptors are internalised while NMDA and AMPA receptors move to the cell surface, so inhibition weakens and excitation strengthens. This explains why benzodiazepines are most effective when given early and lose much of their effect after 20–30 minutes. Prolonged seizures cause hypoxia, lactic acidosis, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis and excitotoxic neuronal death, especially in the hippocampus. Underlying causes in Indian children — fever, neuroinfection, neurocysticercosis, missed medicines and metabolic disturbances — drive recurrence and outcome.

guidedApproach.title: Recognise SE and its causes
guidedApproach.prompt: What should you look for during and after the seizure?
guidedApproach.guidance: Treat any convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes, or repeated seizures without recovery in between, as status epilepticus. While treating, look for clues to the cause: fever and neck stiffness or a bulging fontanelle (meningitis or encephalitis), signs of raised intracranial pressure, trauma, a rash, a known epilepsy with missed doses, or a toxin. After visible jerks stop, check that consciousness improves; persistent eye deviation, nystagmus or subtle twitching with poor responsiveness suggests non-convulsive status epilepticus and needs EEG. Rigors, dystonia from drugs, syncope and psychogenic events can mimic seizures.

guidedApproach.title: Glucose first, then the cause
guidedApproach.prompt: Which tests matter in the first hour?
guidedApproach.guidance: Check capillary glucose immediately and treat a value below 3 mmol/L with 10% dextrose 5 mL/kg. Send electrolytes, calcium, magnesium and a blood gas; correct hyponatraemia and hypocalcaemia, which can sustain seizures. In febrile children, take blood cultures and consider lumbar puncture once the child is stable and there is no contraindication. Image with CT if the child is unstable or has focal signs, and MRI when available. Antiseizure drug levels help in known epilepsy. Continuous EEG is used in the intensive care unit for refractory SE and to detect non-convulsive seizures after anaesthetic infusions.

guidedApproach.title: Treat by the clock
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you treat paediatric SE step by step?
guidedApproach.guidance: At 5 minutes, give a rescue benzodiazepine: buccal or intranasal midazolam 0.1–0.2 mg/kg or rectal diazepam 0.5 mg/kg if there is no IV access, or IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg), repeated once after 5–10 minutes. Do not give more than two benzodiazepine doses. If seizures continue, load one second-line drug: phenytoin 20 mg/kg in saline at 1 mg/kg/min, levetiracetam 20–60 mg/kg, valproate 20–40 mg/kg (avoid in liver or metabolic disease and under 2 years if possible) or phenobarbitone 20 mg/kg. Refractory SE needs intensive care with a midazolam infusion from 1 microgram/kg/min, EEG, and pyridoxine 100 mg IV in infants under 2 years.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 2-year-old boy weighing 12 kg has been convulsing for 15 minutes. He received IV lorazepam 1.2 mg 5 minutes ago and a second dose of 1.2 mg is now due. Glucose is 4.6 mmol/L and he has fever for 2 days. Airway and oxygenation are being supported.
boardQuestions.question: If he is still seizing 5–10 minutes after the second lorazepam dose, what is the next step?

options.explanation: Giving more than two benzodiazepine doses increases respiratory depression without benefit (usual practice).
Treating fever is reasonable but does not stop status epilepticus.
Anaesthetic infusions are for refractory SE in intensive care, after a second-line drug.

options.text: Load a second-line drug, such as levetiracetam 20–60 mg/kg or phenytoin 20 mg/kg
options.explanation: Correct. After two benzodiazepine doses, a second-line drug is given (IAP 2022).
LP is delayed until seizures stop and the child is stable.

boardQuestions.keyPoint: Two benzodiazepine doses, then one second-line drug.

boardQuestions.vignette: An 18-month-old girl with developmental delay is in the PICU with status epilepticus. She has received two doses of lorazepam, phenytoin 20 mg/kg and a midazolam infusion, and seizures continue on EEG. Glucose, sodium and calcium are normal and CSF is normal. She has no fever.
boardQuestions.question: Which additional treatment should be given?

options.text: Pyridoxine 100 mg IV with EEG monitoring
options.explanation: Correct. In infants under 2 years with refractory seizures, a pyridoxine trial is given (LHSC).
Valproate carries a high risk of fatal hepatotoxicity in children under 2, especially with possible metabolic disease (label).
Benzodiazepine boluses are not repeated beyond two doses (IAP 2022).
Oral drugs have no role in refractory status epilepticus.
Stopping the infusion while seizures continue would allow seizures to worsen.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Remember treatable metabolic causes in infants.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Infant with refractory SE: give pyridoxine.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 7-year-old boy with known epilepsy takes oral phenytoin 5 mg/kg/day with good adherence, confirmed by his mother. He presents in status epilepticus during a febrile illness and is still seizing after two IV doses of lorazepam. He weighs 20 kg. His liver function is normal.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most appropriate second-line approach?

options.explanation: IAP advises a half dose when a child already takes up to 6 mg/kg/day of phenytoin, not a full 20 mg/kg load.

options.text: No second-line drug, as he is already on phenytoin
options.explanation: He is still seizing and needs a second-line drug now.

options.text: Phenytoin at half dose (10 mg/kg) or a different second-line drug such as levetiracetam
options.explanation: Correct. On phenytoin up to 6 mg/kg/day, IAP advises a half dose; switching to another second-line drug is also reasonable (IAP 2022).
Propofol is an intensive care treatment for refractory status epilepticus.
Further benzodiazepines are not recommended after two doses.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Adjust loading in children already on an antiseizure medicine.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Already on phenytoin: half load or switch to another second-line drug.

patientEducation: Learn seizure first aid: recovery position, time the seizure, give rescue medicine at 5 minutes (IAP 2022).
lifestyleAndDiet: Regular sleep; supervise swimming and heights.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Neurology review in 2–4 weeks; neurodevelopmental follow-up.

algorithms.title: Convulsive status epilepticus in children: time-based treatment

nodes.text: Convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or more
Airway, oxygen, recovery position; check glucose (dextrose 10% 5 mL/kg if below 3 mmol/L)
Buccal or intranasal midazolam 0.1–0.2 mg/kg, or rectal diazepam 0.5 mg/kg
Observe; find the cause (glucose, electrolytes, infection, imaging)
Secure IV or IO access; one further benzodiazepine, then second-line drug at 20 minutes
IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg); one repeat after 5–10 minutes
Still seizing after two benzodiazepine doses?
Find and treat the cause; monitor for non-convulsive seizures
Phenytoin 20 mg/kg, levetiracetam 20–60 mg/kg, valproate 20–40 mg/kg or phenobarbitone 20 mg/kg
Still seizing after the second-line drug?
Refractory SE: PICU with EEG; midazolam infusion, high-dose phenobarbitone, thiopentone or propofol; pyridoxine 100 mg IV if under 2 years (LHSC dose)
Start maintenance after 8–12 hours; treat the cause
